sentence: This wall has no door.
claim: A venule's lining has no ready-made opening for a white cell: the leukocyte generates its own micron-scale gap or pore as it squeezes through, and this did not need the wall cells to contract (the older view was that the wall cells contract to let it through).
source_title: Barzilai S et al. Leukocytes Breach Endothelial Barriers by Insertion of Nuclear Lobes and Disassembly of Endothelial Actin Filaments. Cell Reports 2017;18(3):685-699 (DOAJ record)
note: Excerpt: 'Leukocytes generate gaps of similar micron-scale size when squeezing through inflamed endothelial barriers in vitro and in vivo ... Gap and pore formation did not require Rho kinase or myosin II-mediated endothelial contractility.' Weizmann coverage: 'Instead of the blood vessel cells contracting to let them through, immune cells squeeze their way through.' 'Door' is a metaphor for a pre-made opening: the wall cells meet edge to edge at junctions (the 'seam' of c13-c14). 'This wall' is the frame-0 venule, a continuous lining; the spleen and the marrow's sinusoids work differently, so the line does not say 'your vessels'. Cross-check: Dictionary.com defines diapedesis as passage through 'unruptured walls'; the claim rests on the paper, not the dictionary. Paid off by name in the whoa (c16).

sentence: It's a neutrophil, your commonest white cell.
claim: In adults, neutrophils are the most numerous circulating white blood cell: about 60-70% of a normal white count of about 4,000-11,000 cells per microlitre.
source_title: Neutrophilia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf (NBK570571)
note: Excerpt: 'In adults, the approximate normal range of white blood cell (WBC) count is 4000 to 11,000 cells/microL, out of which 60% to 70% are mature neutrophils circulating in peripheral blood.' Sources differ on the share (BioNumbers 100511: 60%, range 50-70%, Sell 2001; StatPearls Leukocytosis NBK560882: 40-60%), but neutrophils are the commonest type in every range, so the line says 'your commonest', with no share voiced. Adult ranges: in young children lymphocytes can outnumber them. Replaces the bible's S21 address (statpearls article-31353), which never came up in research.

sentence: About eight micrometres across, a little wider than a red cell.
claim: A neutrophil suspended in fluid (round, roughly as in blood) measures about 8.3-8.4 µm across (range about 7.3-9.7 µm), the largest leukocyte type in that study.
source_title: BioNumbers (Harvard Medical School) ID 100510: neutrophil diameter (Downey et al. 1990)
note: Excerpt: '8.4 µm (range 7.3 to 9.7 µm) ... Neutrophils were the largest cells with a mean diameter of 8.3µm'. Isolated cells, measured by Coulter counter and flow cytometry; PMC3605679 gives 7-8 µm, consistent. The bible's 12-15 µm (StatPearls 31353) is a cell flattened on a smear, so the scale pill badges 'round, in blood'.

sentence: About eight micrometres across, a little wider than a red cell.
claim: A red blood cell is about 7.5 µm across, so a round neutrophil (about 8.3 µm, c3) is a little wider; on a stained slide a neutrophil looks clearly bigger than the red cells around it.
source_title: White Blood cells - The Histology Guide - University of Leeds
note: Excerpt: neutrophils are '12-14 µm diameter, and so look bigger than the surrounding red blood cells' (a smear). The 7.5 µm red-cell figure came from the research summary of this source, not from the quoted excerpt, and this session's proxy refuses the host, so the page is still unopened: confirm it there. Cross-check: episode 1's ledger (c2) gives 7-8 µm for a red cell and voiced 'about seven micrometers', so 'a little wider' (8.3 / 7.5 = 1.1, computed) stays consistent across the series, where 'a red cell's width' would not. Width only: the red cell is a thin disc, so the neutrophil has far more bulk.

sentence: Under a sore fingertip, white cells gather.
claim: At a site of tissue damage, widened, leakier vessels let fluid, proteins and white blood cells move out of the circulation into the damaged tissue.
source_title: How Is Inflammation Involved in Swelling? (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
note: Excerpt: 'Increased blood vessel permeability allows fluid, proteins, and white blood cells to migrate from the circulation to the site of tissue damage.' The sore fingertip is that site, stylised: a swelling and a soft glow, no wound or blood, and no colour voiced (redness reads differently on different skin tones). 'Gather' is the white cells collecting in that tissue. Sets up pus before the change names it. Described as how the body works, with no care advice.

sentence: Rudolf Virchow taught that pus grew from the injured tissue itself.
claim: Virchow and some of his followers held that pus cells originated inside the injured tissue's own connective-tissue cells ('connective tissue corpuscles'), not in the blood.
source_title: Cohnheim and Virchows Views of the Origin of Pus-Corpuscles: English Reports of the Same (PMC6108650)
note: Excerpt: 'the origin of pus-cells, which Virchow and some of his followers had represented as originating in the interior of connective tissue corpuscles'. This page was the top hit of an exact-phrase search, but the tool did not confirm which 19th-century reprint carries the text (the other hit: PMC6088652), and this session's proxy refuses ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, so it is still unopened. Open it and confirm before locking; the unnamed fallback lines are in the script's Notes. 'Taught', not 'was wrong': Stricker (1868, PMC10004891) argued that some pus cells still come from tissue. 'The injured tissue itself' simplifies 'its connective-tissue cells'.

sentence: In eighteen sixty-seven, his own assistant, Julius Cohnheim, watched a living frog's vessels.
claim: Cohnheim was an assistant at Berlin University's pathological institute under Virchow (Wikipedia: autumn 1864-1868; Britannica: 1865-68); his 1867 essay on inflammation and suppuration, published in Virchow's Archiv, established his reputation.
source_title: Julius Friedrich Cohnheim (Wikipedia)
note: Excerpt: 'Cohnheim became an assistant at Berlin University's pathological institute under Virchow in the fall of 1864, and stayed until 1868 ... His 1867 essay on inflammation and suppuration, published in Virchow's archive, is the work that established his reputation.' The start year differs by one between sources; he was in post in 1867 under both, so 'his own assistant' holds. No start year is voiced. Split from the old 22-word sentence so it passes the breath test.

sentence: In eighteen sixty-seven, his own assistant, Julius Cohnheim, watched a living frog's vessels.
claim: Cohnheim exposed the mesentery of a living frog paralysed with curare ('woorara') and watched its vessels under the microscope.
source_title: Passage of Sanguineous Corpuscles through the Walls of the Vessels, Etc (PMC9799538)
note: Excerpt: 'He demonstrated directly the passage of white and red corpuscles through the vascular walls of the frog mesentery.' The frog was paralysed with 'woorara' (curare), so alive. 'A living frog's vessels' are the vessels of the mesentery, the thin membrane that holds the gut. A translated 19th-century account.

sentence: White cells were climbing out.
claim: In Cohnheim's frog, white cells seemed glued to the inside of the vessel wall, pressed into it, lodged in pockets and spread out into the surrounding tissue.
source_title: Passage of Sanguineous Corpuscles through the Walls of the Vessels, Etc (PMC9799538)
note: Excerpt: 'The white corpuscles, which seem glued to the internal face of the wall of the vessel, depress this wall, lodge in pockets, and spread into surrounding tissues.' 'Climbing out' stands for pressing into the wall and spreading into the tissue. The same page carries Beale's dissent that white cells and pus cells differ.

sentence: White cells were climbing out.
claim: By 1867 Cohnheim had confirmed earlier suspicions that in inflammation leukocytes pass through capillary walls into the tissues.
source_title: Julius Cohnheim (Encyclopaedia Britannica, print view)
note: Excerpt: 'by 1867, he confirmed earlier suspicions that the condition results from the passage of leukocytes (white blood corpuscles) through capillary walls and into tissues'. 'Confirmed earlier suspicions', so the film never says he was first. The end card's fact: Augustus Waller, 'Microscopic Observations on the Perforation of the Capillaries by the Corpuscles of the Blood', Philosophical Magazine, November 1846, 29: 397-405 (historyofmedicine.com, Garrison-Morton); '21 years before' is 1867 - 1846 (computed). Whonamedit credits William Addison (1843), so the card says 'saw', not 'first'; PMC10022970 says Waller 'had not the good fortune to attract attention to his discovery'.

sentence: Sticky molecules on the wall catch it, and it rolls.
claim: Selectins on the endothelium (the vessel's lining) tether passing leukocytes and make them roll.
source_title: PMC review on selectin and integrin signalling in leukocyte recruitment (PMC4592324)
note: Excerpt: 'Endothelial selectins initiate tethering and rolling of leukocytes.' 'Sticky molecules on the wall' are the endothelial selectins. This step needs no CD18, so in LAD-I (c15) the cells still roll: the ghost pass draws them rolling. The search result did not show the article's title, so the source title is descriptive. The rolling speed is a mouse figure, shown only in the picture (see Notes).

sentence: Its own grips switch on, and it stops.
claim: Signals from engaged selectins and chemokines activate beta-2 integrins on the leukocyte, which mediate slow rolling and arrest.
source_title: PMC review on selectin and integrin signalling in leukocyte recruitment (PMC4592324)
note: Excerpt: 'Signals from engaged selectins and chemokines activate β2 integrins that mediate slow rolling and arrest.' 'Its own grips' are the white cell's β2 integrins (built on CD18), which grip ICAM-1 on the wall (Phillipson 2006). Ley 2007: capture, rolling, then arrest. 'Its own' against 'on the wall' keeps the wall's molecules and the cell's apart, as the cascade does.

sentence: It crawls to a seam between two wall cells.
claim: After arrest, neutrophils crawl along the inside of the vessel to distant emigration sites, using the integrin Mac-1 gripping ICAM-1; cells that cannot crawl start to transmigrate close to where they stopped and are slower to get out.
source_title: Phillipson M et al. Intraluminal crawling of neutrophils to emigration sites: a molecularly distinct process from adhesion in the recruitment cascade. J Exp Med 2006;203(12):2569
note: Mouse intravital work. Only the title is verbatim; the rest summarises the abstract. A follow-up Vav1 study says crawling often heads toward a junction between wall cells, and a review (PMC2882030) says Mac-1 crawling moves the cell toward preferred junctions. 'Seam' means an endothelial junction. Mac-1 is itself a β2 integrin, so 'those grips' (c15) covers the crawl too.

sentence: It crawls to a seam between two wall cells.
claim: Most neutrophils leave between two endothelial cells (paracellular); in mouse venules 60-85 µm wide, fewer than 15% went through a single wall cell (transcellular).
source_title: Xia et al. Conditions that promote transcellular neutrophil migration in vivo. Scientific Reports 2024 (PMC11196655)
note: Excerpt: 'less than 15% of neutrophils extravasated transcellularly in WT mice'. A relayed excerpt on the same study gives about 90% paracellular in the mouse cremaster. Mouse data. The line follows this one cell on the usual route and does not say 'all'; a minority go straight through one wall cell (Ley 2007 lists both routes).

sentence: In a rare inherited condition, those grips fail: white cells struggle to leave.
claim: In leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, a rare inherited condition (incidence estimated at about 1 in a million), mutations in CD18, the shared subunit of the beta-2 integrins, stop leukocytes migrating out to infection sites; blood white counts are typically high because the cells can't move into tissue, and pus often fails to form.
source_title: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency - StatPearls (point-of-care 24214)
note: Relayed excerpts (the full text is behind registration): 'Leukocytes cannot migrate to infection sites to kill invading microorganisms due to mutations in the CD18 glycoprotein'; counts are typically elevated; 'no pus'. Wikipedia LAD-1: neutrophils are 'unable to adhere to and migrate out of blood vessels, so their counts can be high'. 'Those grips' are the β2 integrins of c12-c13. 'Struggle' hedges severity: one case report with complete CD18 loss still formed some pus. Drawn as LAD-I works: the cells still roll (c11) but tumble on without stopping. Placed after the crawl so roll, stop, crawl run unbroken. Not named on air; no talk of infection, treatment or immunity (bible §9, Ep 6).

sentence: This one wedges its nucleus into the seam, making its own door.
claim: Leukocytes breach the vessel lining by inserting lobes of their nucleus into their leading edge at the junction and generating micron-scale gaps themselves, together with local disassembly of the wall cells' actin filaments; the gaps did not need the wall cells to contract.
source_title: Barzilai S et al. Leukocytes Breach Endothelial Barriers by Insertion of Nuclear Lobes and Disassembly of Endothelial Actin Filaments. Cell Reports 2017;18(3):685-699 (DOAJ record)
note: Excerpt: 'Nuclear squeezing involved either preexistent or de novo-generated lobes inserted into the leukocyte lamellipodia ... Gap and pore formation did not require Rho kinase or myosin II-mediated endothelial contractility.' Weizmann coverage: 'Using their nuclei to exert force, they insert themselves between - as well as into - the cells in the vessel walls.' 'Making its own door' pays off c1 and follows the paper's 'leukocytes generate gaps'; the wall's actin also gives way (the title), drawn thinning at the seam. 'Lumpy' is gone: the nucleus is drawn lobed (3-5 lobes, StatPearls 31353), not voiced.

sentence: It pours through a gap narrower than itself.
claim: The gaps leukocytes open between wall cells are micron-scale (a few micrometres), narrower than the round neutrophil's roughly 8 µm (c3).
source_title: Barzilai S et al. Leukocytes Breach Endothelial Barriers by Insertion of Nuclear Lobes and Disassembly of Endothelial Actin Filaments. Cell Reports 2017;18(3):685-699 (DOAJ record)
note: Excerpt: 'Mononuclear and polymorphonuclear leukocytes generate gaps of similar micron-scale size when squeezing through inflamed endothelial barriers.' The comparison with c3 (about 8 µm) is computed. The 4-5 µm figure comes only from press coverage (Labroots), so the readout says 'a few µm'. A review (PMC3605679) has neutrophils (7-8 µm) passing capillaries as narrow as about 2 µm. 'Pours' is the bible's whoa verb.

sentence: Around it, the wall pulls tight.
claim: As a neutrophil crosses, local RhoA signalling in the wall cell builds contractile F-actin structures around it, which confine the pore it opened and stop plasma leaking out through it.
source_title: Heemskerk N et al. F-actin-rich contractile endothelial pores prevent vascular leakage during leukocyte diapedesis through local RhoA signalling. Nat Commun 2016;7:10493
note: Relayed excerpt: 'local RhoA activation starts the assembly of contractile F-actin structures around emigrating neutrophils, which confine the neutrophil-induced endothelial pore and stop plasma leakage.' Mostly cultured wall cells, with in vivo support. 'Pulls tight' is the pore confined around the cell; it does not claim an inflamed vessel never leaks (c5: inflamed vessels grow leakier), so no 'no leak' is said or shown. Drawn as the wall's edges cinching at the cell's waist, with no ring (theme.json no_circle).

sentence: So pus mostly comes from your blood.
claim: Pus is an exudate chiefly made of dead white blood cells (such as neutrophils), plus tissue debris and microbes.
source_title: Pus - Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster (medical definition)
note: Excerpt: 'composed of exudate chiefly containing dead white blood cells (as neutrophils), tissue debris, and pathogenic microorganisms (as bacteria)'. Those white cells came out of the blood (c9-c10, c20-c21), hence 'mostly comes from your blood'; 'mostly' covers the debris and microbes. A dictionary, not a clinical source; pus is spoken, never shown, and nothing is advised.

sentence: So pus mostly comes from your blood.
claim: Pus consists mainly of the debris formed by the disintegration of leukocytes that passed out through the capillary walls (Cohnheim's conclusion, as Britannica gives it).
source_title: Julius Cohnheim (Encyclopaedia Britannica, print view)
note: Excerpt: '... and that pus consists mainly of the debris formed by disintegration of these leukocytes.' 'These leukocytes' are the ones that crossed the capillary walls into the tissue (c10). Stricker argued that some pus cells come from tissue (PMC10004891), which 'mostly' allows for. It answers the change's wrong idea (c6).

sentence: White cells that rolled, stopped, crawled and squeezed out.
claim: Leukocytes leave the blood in a cascade: capture and rolling, activation and arrest, crawling along the inside of the vessel, then migration through the wall, between wall cells (paracellular) or through one (transcellular).
source_title: Ley K, Laudanna C, Cybulsky MI, Nourshargh S. Getting to the site of inflammation: the leukocyte adhesion cascade updated. Nat Rev Immunol 2007;7(9):678-89 (PubMed 17717539; bible S22)
note: Excerpt: 'The traditional three steps of rolling, activation and firm adhesion have recently been augmented and refined. Slow rolling, adhesion strengthening, intraluminal crawling and paracellular and transcellular migration are now recognized as separate, additional steps.' Key points: 'starting with capture and followed by rolling and arrest.' Bible S22; the line is the bible's takeaway in four verbs. Beyond the lining the cell also passes a basement membrane, not voiced.

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, your bone marrow made new neutrophils.
claim: The bone marrow makes neutrophils continuously, at a basal rate of about 5 x 10^10 to 10 x 10^10 a day.
source_title: Summers C et al. Neutrophil kinetics in health and disease. Trends Immunol 2010;31(8):318-324 (PMC2930213)
note: Excerpt: 'Neutrophil abundance, coupled with their brief (6-8 h) circulating half life, mandates a basal rate of production by the bone marrow of 5 × 10^10-10 × 10^10 neutrophils/day.' Britannica gives about 100 billion a day for a normal adult. A resting adult's basal rate, not a verdict on any viewer.

sentence: More than thirty million.
claim: At the low end of the basal rate, 5 x 10^10 a day, the marrow makes about 579,000 neutrophils a second: more than thirty million within the film's first 52 seconds, and about 36-39 million while the line is spoken.
source_title: Summers C et al. Neutrophil kinetics in health and disease. Trends Immunol 2010;31(8):318-324 (PMC2930213)
note: Computed: 5 × 10^10 / 86,400 s = 578,704 a second, the tally's rate from frame 0, badged 'low estimate'. It passes 30 million at 30,000,000 / 578,704 = 51.8 s. The meanwhile line is planned for about 62.1-67.2 s: 35.9-38.9 million at the low end and 71.9-77.8 million at the high end (10^11 a day, 1,157,407 a second), so 'more than thirty million' holds at both. Cross-check: Dancey et al. give 0.85 × 10^9 per kg a day, about 6 × 10^10 for 70 kg, about 690,000 a second (computed). It holds down to about 3.9 × 10^10 a day; the fallback 'Tens of millions.' holds down to about 1.3 × 10^10 (computed). The circulating lifespan is not voiced, since it is disputed (about 6-8 h against about 5.4 days).
